Polar Jupiter orbiter; first solar-powered spacecraft to reach Jupiter (~50 m² triple-junction solar arrays delivering ~14 kW at Earth, ~500 W at Jupiter)

© NASA / JPL-Caltech / Southwest Research Institute — U.S. Government work, public domain. Juno is the first spacecraft to enter a polar orbit around Jupiter, allowing it to map the planet's magnetic field, gravity field, and atmospheric chemistry below the cloud tops. Highly elliptical 53-day orbit takes it from inside the radiation belts (perijove ~4200 km above cloud tops) out past Callisto's distance. Confirmed Jupiter has a 'diluted' rocky core (not a sharp boundary), measured the polar cyclone configuration (eight circumpolar storms around the north pole, five, later six, around the south), imaged Io's volcanism in unprecedented detail (close-pass 2023-12-30, ~1500 km altitude). Mission extension through September 2025 includes flybys of all four Galilean moons.

Cape Canaveral, 2011-08-05. Juno is the first solar-powered spacecraft to reach Jupiter — three massive solar arrays span 20 m tip-to-tip, generating 14 kW at Earth distance but only ~500 W at Jupiter (5.4 AU). The polar orbit was chosen to minimise time inside Jupiter's lethal radiation belts.

Closest approach 559 km on 2013-10-09. The flyby added 7.3 km/s to Juno's heliocentric velocity — the boost needed to reach Jupiter directly (a Hohmann transfer from Earth would have required a far larger launch vehicle than the Atlas V provides).

2016-07-05 UTC (July 4 Pacific time — Independence Day in the US). 35-minute main engine burn slowed Juno from hyperbolic to a highly-elliptical 53-day polar orbit, threading the gap between Jupiter and its main radiation belts. The polar orbit is unique among Jupiter missions — letting Juno map the deep interior + auroras while limiting total radiation dose. Mission extended through 2025.
First polar orbiter of Jupiter; solar-powered beyond the asteroid belt for the first time

Juno entered Jupiter orbit 2016-07-05 on a highly elliptical 53-day polar trajectory that takes it from inside the radiation belts (perijove ~4200 km above cloud tops) out past Callisto. Solar-powered — its ~50 m² triple-junction arrays deliver 14 kW at Earth but only ~500 W at Jupiter, the first time solar power has been used at that distance. Confirmed Jupiter has a diluted rocky core (not a sharp boundary), measured the polar cyclone arrangement (eight circumpolar storms around the north pole, five, later six, around the south), and imaged Io’s volcanism at unprecedented detail in 2023. Extended mission includes flybys of all four Galilean moons through 2025.
